title: Playing at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn through Sunday #theatre #b...
transcript: From the guy that brought you Dorian Gray with Sarah Snook and Dracula with Cynthia Erivo comes another classic reimagined to be about modern influencer culture, starring actors you might recognize like Yerin Ha from Bridgerton and Phia Saban from house of the Dragon. This is a modern retelling of Jean Genet's 1947 play The Maids, about a pair of sisters who work as housemaids for a cruel, vain woman. And overall, I think I appreciated what Kip Williams did as the director of this production more than as the adapter of the script. Cause like, on a superficial level, it evoked a lot of what it was meant to evoke: the suspense in the plot, and the palpable tension between characters used to illustrate the power dynamics between the wealthy and the working class. And I thought the acting was pretty strong all around, especially from the one actor you might not have heard of, Lydia Wilson. But Williams's adaptation of the script had several fundamental issues for me, most of them relating to the character of Madame played by Yerin Ha. First of all, if the point is about weaponizing her wealth and power against the people who serve her, I don't know that making her a lifestyle influencer was the most intuitive equivalent to modern day. It's not that it doesn't make any sense, but I wonder if making her a tech billionaire or like a Waspy socialite might have been a more effective commentary on modern class Disparity. I didn't see Dracula, by the way, but between this and Dorian Grey, it seems clear that the topic of social media and, like, filtering the world through a screen is something that greatly interests Kip Williams. But when it comes to the connections he's drawing in this play, I see what he's reaching for, but it does feel like a reach. The production seems more interested in cramming modern slang and TikTok buzzwords into the dialogue within an inch of its life, reminding us incessantly that it takes place in our current moment without having much to say about it. Last thing I'll say is that the way that he depicts this woman's obsession with makeup, plastic surgery, Snapchat filters and fashionable clothing was, like, conflated with her cruelty in a way that seemed a little problematic. It's not that there's nothing to explore there, but it's a complicated issue in terms of how gender and patriarchal beauty standards intersect with class. But he seems kinda unwilling to engage with those thorny nuances. So I thought his interpretation of this villain had a bit of an air of misogyny around it on top of everything else.
reasoning: Reviewer praises the direction, acting, and atmosphere but has substantial criticisms of the adaptation's script, its modern framing, and what he perceives as a misogynistic undertone. The critique outweighs the praise but doesn't reach outright dismissal.
keyQuote: I see what he's reaching for, but it does feel like a reach.
